The core conflict arises from Heritage Kitchener's position that the owners are obligated to
construct a replica Belfry and from their proposed mechanism to enforce this requirement,
namely the demand for a heritage easement agreement under the Section 37 of the Ontario
Heritage Act.
Section 37 allows municipalities to enter easement agreements to conserve designated heritage
property, but it does not impose a statutory duty on owners to reconstruct lost heritage
attributes.
Easements are voluntary agreements intended to protect existing heritage attributes and
are typically permanent and run with the land.
It is our view that requiring a permanent heritage easement is a disproportionate and inappropriate
response to what is fundamentally a site-specific permit-based approval under the Section 33
of the Ontario Heritage Act, which governs heritage permits.
Even assuming that the reconstruction request was reasonable, Section 33 requires that conditions
of approval relate directly to the proposed work.
Attaching a permanent easement as a condition to a permit of demolition is beyond what the
legislation contemplates.
Despite the application being under review since May 14th, Heritage Kitchener has not
provided any draft easement agreement, no proposed terms or wording. Heritage easements are serious
legal instruments registered on title. They are typically permanent, run with the land,
and are often viewed as encumbrances by lenders and prospective purchasers.
Without reviewing the actual document proposed by the City, we have no ability to assess how or when

the shed. These demolitions are unrelated and could have been completed without interfering
with the belfry in its last location on the roof of the building. For all these reasons,
we respectfully submit that the imposed condition is unreasonable, disproportionate,
and unsupported by the Ontario Heritage Act.
